1. Core Clinical Tension: A 62-year-old diabetic male from Tamil Nadu presents with a 2-week history of fever, acute left upper quadrant and epigastric pain, and abdominal imaging demonstrating focal distal pancreatic swelling and acute splenic vein thrombosis with collaterals, yet serum amylase and lipase are completely normal. The critical diagnostic challenge is differentiating this infectious pancreatic thrombophlebitis from acute pancreatitis, occult pancreatic malignancy, or unprovoked deep splanchnic venous thrombosis.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint occurs following abdominal CECT and MRI confirming focal inflammatory changes in the pancreatic body/tail and acute splenic vein thrombosis in the context of normal pancreatic enzymes, strictly prior to blood culture Gram staining, colony morphology, and automated identification.
3. Differential Distinctions: Acute edematous or necrotizing pancreatitis is excluded by persistently normal serum amylase and lipase levels. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is ruled out by the acute febrile course, lack of a focal discrete mass or ductal cutoff, and bacteremia with resolution under targeted antimicrobial therapy. Primary thrombophilia is excluded by localized peripancreatic inflammatory phlegmon and blood culture isolation.
case_prompt:
A 62-year-old male from Tamil Nadu, India, presented with a 2-week history of fever and acute onset of abdominal pain for 4 days. He had a medical history of chronic diabetes mellitus and hypertension, for which he was noncompliant with medications.

On physical examination, the patient was febrile and tachycardic with a pulse rate of 105 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 148/90 mmHg. Abdominal examination revealed marked tenderness localized to the left hypochondrium and epigastrium without peritoneal signs. Examination of the other systems was unremarkable.

Initial laboratory evaluation demonstrated a normal complete blood count, normal renal function tests, and normal liver function parameters. Serum amylase and lipase levels were completely within normal limits. His hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) was 9.2%, indicating poor glycemic control. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) scan of the abdomen revealed a mildly bulky distal body and tail of the pancreas with surrounding peripancreatic fat stranding. The retropancreatic portion of the splenic vein was distended with a non-enhancing intraluminal thrombus and vessel wall enhancement, suggestive of acute thrombosis. Prominent venous collaterals were noted in periportal, peripancreatic, omental, and retroperitoneal distributions. The head, neck, and proximal body of the pancreas were normal, without dilation of the main pancreatic or common bile ducts; mild splenomegaly was present. An abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan confirmed mild distal pancreatic enlargement and demonstrated a T2-hyperintense thrombus with restricted diffusion in the retropancreatic splenic vein.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Epigastric pain radiating to the back with peripancreatic fat stranding mimicked typical acute pancreatitis, but serum amylase and lipase levels were completely normal, directing suspicion toward an infectious inflammatory phlegmon.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: His blood investigations showed normal hemogram, serum amylase, and lipase levels... In view of the history of fever with normal amylase and lipase levels, the possibility of infective cause of pancreatic inflammation with splenic vein thrombosis was postulated.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Focal enlargement of the pancreatic body and tail with contiguous splenic vein occlusion and collaterals in an older diabetic patient strongly suggested pancreatic malignancy, but the absence of a distinct mass or ductal dilation and the presence of high fevers favored an acute infectious process.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The head, neck, and proximal body of the pancreas were normal. The main pancreatic and common bile ducts were not dilated... In view of the history of fever with normal amylase and lipase levels, the possibility of infective cause of pancreatic inflammation with splenic vein thrombosis was postulated.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Primary Splanchnic Vein Thrombosis / Hypercoagulable State
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Isolated splenic vein thrombosis can occur spontaneously in thrombophilic states, but the localized peripancreatic phlegmon and systemic fever demonstrated that the thrombosis was secondary to septic thrombophlebitis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The retro-pancreatic portion of the splenic vein was distended with non-enhancing intraluminal thrombus and vessel wall enhancement, suggestive of acute thrombosis... In view of the history of fever with normal amylase and lipase levels, the possibility of infective cause of pancreatic inflammation with splenic vein thrombosis was postulated.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Blood cultures drawn on admission revealed Gram-negative bacilli exhibiting characteristic bipolar 'safety-pin' Gram staining and metallic sheen colonies on MacConkey agar, identified by the VITEK2 automated system as Burkholderia pseudomallei, confirming pancreatic melioidosis complicated by acute septic splenic vein thrombosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Blood culture from this patient revealed a safety pin appearance of Gram-negative bacilli in the routine Gram staining [Figure 3a], and colonies showed a metallic sheen on MacConkey's agar plate [Figure 3b]. After an incubation period of 72 h, using the VITEK2 (Biomerieux) automated system, the causative agent was revealed to be B. pseudomallei.

editor_comments: Distilled successfully according to the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology. Zero spoilers or pathogen names in case_prompt. Breakpoint set prior to blood culture Gram stain and automated microbiological identification. Verbatim quotes support all differential candidates and the diagnostic pivot.
